The engine's lines for 150 positions from your games: what your move allowed, what was better, and the pattern to practise. On the boards, red is your move and green the engine's choice.

Repeated mistake

2...Nc6 better 2...cxd4

12% winning chances lost · you played it in 17 games

After 2...Nc6, Stockfish's answer is 3.d5 Nb8 4.f4 g6. Stockfish rates the line −1.53 for you, against −0.19 after 2...cxd4: 3.d5 hits your knight with a pawn and it has to move again (3...Nb8), so you lose time; 2...cxd4 first takes the pawn that chases it. Next time, before you put a piece on a square, check whether a pawn can chase it away with a gain of time.

What 2...Nc6 allows
2...Nc6 3.d5 Nb8 4.f4 g6 5.Nc3 Bg7 6.Nf3 d6 7.a4 Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 Nf6 9.Qd3 O-O 10.Be2 … (−1.53 for you)
Better: 2...cxd4
2...cxd4 3.Nf3 e5 4.c3 Nc6 5.cxd4 exd4 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Nc3 Bb4 8.Nxc6 bxc6 9.Bd3 d5 10.exd5 … (−0.19 for you)

About piece activity: A piece is worth what it can do: how many squares it reaches matters more than its point value. Put your pieces where they have the most scope, and look for ways to cut an enemy piece off from the fight; a bishop or knight shut out of play is almost a piece less. Lasker, Chess Strategy (Project Gutenberg #5614), Chapter III, General Principles of Chess Strategy: Mobility ↗

Repeated mistake

1...e5 better 1...d5

9.1% winning chances lost · you played it in 15 games

After 1...e5, Stockfish's answer is 2.dxe5 d5 3.Nf3 Ne7 4.Bf4. Stockfish rates the line −1.26 for you, against −0.32 after 1...d5: 2.dxe5 takes the pawn on e5, which one white piece attacks and none of yours defends. Next time, count the attackers and defenders of every pawn and piece before you move.

What 1...e5 allows

3...e6 better 3...cxd4

12% winning chances lost · you played it in 11 games

After 3...e6, Stockfish's answer is 4.d5 Na5 5.d6 b6. Stockfish rates the line −1.82 for you, against −0.36 after 3...cxd4: a few moves later you stand 0.30 pawns worse on space and 0.28 on threats. Next time, ask whether your move gives your opponent room to expand.

What 3...e6 allows
3...e6 4.d5 Na5 5.d6 b6 6.Nc3 a6 7.e5 Bb7 8.Bd3 f5 9.Qe2 b5 10.Bg5 Qb6 11.Bxf5 … (−1.82 for you)
Better: 3...cxd4
3...cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5 5.Nb5 d6 6.N1c3 Nf6 7.Bg5 a6 8.Na3 b5 9.Bxf6 gxf6 10.Nd5 f5 11.Bd3 … (−0.36 for you)

About space: Control of the centre gives you space: your pieces can switch quickly between the wings while your opponent's stay cramped behind their own pawns. Capablanca counts the four centre squares and notes that no violent attack succeeds without control of at least two of them. Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (Project Gutenberg #33870), Chapter I, First Principles: 7. Control of the Centre ↗

5...e5 better 5...Nf6

11% winning chances lost · you played it in 10 games

After 5...e5, Stockfish's answer is 6.Ndb5 a6 7.Nd6+ Bxd6. Stockfish rates the line −1.57 for you, against −0.39 after 5...Nf6: White's knight gets to d6 (7.Nd6+), a square no pawn of yours can cover, and a few moves later you stand 1.17 pawns worse on king safety. Next time, ask which squares in your camp no pawn of yours can cover any more, and which enemy piece can reach them.

What 5...e5 allows
5...e5 6.Ndb5 a6 7.Nd6+ Bxd6 8.Qxd6 Qe7 9.Qd1 Nf6 10.Bg5 d6 11.Nd5 Qd8 12.Bxf6 gxf6 13.Qf3 … (−1.57 for you)
Better: 5...Nf6
5...Nf6 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.e5 Nd5 8.Ne4 Qc7 9.f4 Qa5+ 10.Bd2 Qb6 11.Bd3 Nb4 12.Qe2 Rb8 13.b3 … (−0.39 for you)
  • you lose the bishop pair
  • b6 and d5 become holes in your camp (no pawn of yours can cover them)

About king safety: Your king is safest behind pawns that haven't moved: each pawn you push in front of it stops guarding squares the enemy pieces can then use for a direct attack, and the pushed pawn itself becomes a target. Castle early, and move those pawns only for a concrete reason, not to stop a pin that isn't there yet. Opening: D10 Slav Defense

What masters and players near your level play here

Originally considered a less-orthodox defence in the Queen's Gambit, this opening has stood as an entire opening system in its own right for decades. The idea behind this defence is straightforward: instead of locking in the light squared bishop on c8, why not support the center with the c-pawn instead?

6...c4 better 6...Bb7

10% winning chances lost · you played it in 5 games

After 6...c4, Stockfish's answer is 7.d3 b4 8.axb4 cxd3. Stockfish rates the line −0.78 for you, against +0.41 after 6...Bb7: a few moves later you stand 0.49 pawns worse on piece activity, and you get an isolated pawn on a6. Next time, ask which of your pieces your move leaves with fewer squares.

What 6...c4 allows
6...c4 7.d3 b4 8.axb4 cxd3 9.cxd3 Nxb4 10.Bb1 Nf6 11.d4 Bb7 12.e5 Nfd5 13.Ng5 Qc7 14.Qh5 … (−0.78 for you)
Better: 6...Bb7
6...Bb7 7.d3 Qc7 8.O-O Nf6 9.Ne2 Bd6 10.c4 O-O 11.h3 h6 12.Re1 Rfd8 13.Rb1 Rab8 14.Be3 … (+0.41 for you)
  • you get an isolated pawn on a6

About piece activity: A piece is worth what it can do: how many squares it reaches matters more than its point value. Put your pieces where they have the most scope, and look for ways to cut an enemy piece off from the fight; a bishop or knight shut out of play is almost a piece less. Lasker, Chess Strategy (Project Gutenberg #5614), Chapter III, General Principles of Chess Strategy: Mobility ↗

Why these moves go wrong · Bullet only

The engine's lines for 3 positions from your games: what your move allowed, what was better, and the pattern to practise. On the boards, red is your move and green the engine's choice.

Repeated mistake

5...e5 better 5...Nf6

11% winning chances lost · you played it in 10 games

After 5...e5, Stockfish's answer is 6.Ndb5 a6 7.Nd6+ Bxd6. Stockfish rates the line −1.57 for you, against −0.39 after 5...Nf6: White's knight gets to d6 (7.Nd6+), a square no pawn of yours can cover, and a few moves later you stand 1.17 pawns worse on king safety. Next time, ask which squares in your camp no pawn of yours can cover any more, and which enemy piece can reach them.

What 5...e5 allows
5...e5 6.Ndb5 a6 7.Nd6+ Bxd6 8.Qxd6 Qe7 9.Qd1 Nf6 10.Bg5 d6 11.Nd5 Qd8 12.Bxf6 gxf6 13.Qf3 … (−1.57 for you)
Better: 5...Nf6
5...Nf6 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.e5 Nd5 8.Ne4 Qc7 9.f4 Qa5+ 10.Bd2 Qb6 11.Bd3 Nb4 12.Qe2 Rb8 13.b3 … (−0.39 for you)
  • you lose the bishop pair
  • b6 and d5 become holes in your camp (no pawn of yours can cover them)

About king safety: Your king is safest behind pawns that haven't moved: each pawn you push in front of it stops guarding squares the enemy pieces can then use for a direct attack, and the pushed pawn itself becomes a target. Castle early, and move those pawns only for a concrete reason, not to stop a pin that isn't there yet. Lasker, Chess Strategy (Project Gutenberg #5614), Chapter VI, The Middle Game: Breaking up the King's Side ↗

Repeated mistake

3...e6 better 3...cxd4

12% winning chances lost · you played it in 11 games

After 3...e6, Stockfish's answer is 4.d5 Na5 5.d6 b6. Stockfish rates the line −1.82 for you, against −0.36 after 3...cxd4: a few moves later you stand 0.30 pawns worse on space and 0.28 on threats. Next time, ask whether your move gives your opponent room to expand.

What 3...e6 allows
3...e6 4.d5 Na5 5.d6 b6 6.Nc3 a6 7.e5 Bb7 8.Bd3 f5 9.Qe2 b5 10.Bg5 Qb6 11.Bxf5 … (−1.82 for you)
Better: 3...cxd4
3...cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5 5.Nb5 d6 6.N1c3 Nf6 7.Bg5 a6 8.Na3 b5 9.Bxf6 gxf6 10.Nd5 f5 11.Bd3 … (−0.36 for you)

About space: Control of the centre gives you space: your pieces can switch quickly between the wings while your opponent's stay cramped behind their own pawns. Capablanca counts the four centre squares and notes that no violent attack succeeds without control of at least two of them. Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (Project Gutenberg #33870), Chapter I, First Principles: 7. Control of the Centre ↗

Why these moves go wrong · Blitz only

The engine's lines for 3 positions from your games: what your move allowed, what was better, and the pattern to practise. On the boards, red is your move and green the engine's choice.

Repeated mistake

2...Nc6 better 2...cxd4

12% winning chances lost · you played it in 17 games

After 2...Nc6, Stockfish's answer is 3.d5 Nb8 4.f4 g6. Stockfish rates the line −1.53 for you, against −0.19 after 2...cxd4: 3.d5 hits your knight with a pawn and it has to move again (3...Nb8), so you lose time; 2...cxd4 first takes the pawn that chases it. Next time, before you put a piece on a square, check whether a pawn can chase it away with a gain of time.

What 2...Nc6 allows
2...Nc6 3.d5 Nb8 4.f4 g6 5.Nc3 Bg7 6.Nf3 d6 7.a4 Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 Nf6 9.Qd3 O-O 10.Be2 … (−1.53 for you)
Better: 2...cxd4
2...cxd4 3.Nf3 e5 4.c3 Nc6 5.cxd4 exd4 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Nc3 Bb4 8.Nxc6 bxc6 9.Bd3 d5 10.exd5 … (−0.19 for you)

About piece activity: A piece is worth what it can do: how many squares it reaches matters more than its point value. Put your pieces where they have the most scope, and look for ways to cut an enemy piece off from the fight; a bishop or knight shut out of play is almost a piece less. Lasker, Chess Strategy (Project Gutenberg #5614), Chapter III, General Principles of Chess Strategy: Mobility ↗

Observation · How games end

You abandoned 11 games, and each one costs rating points

You abandoned 11 of your 320 games (your opponents abandoned 11). Each one counts as a full loss and costs rating points in rated games. Going by the ratings you could have expected about 5.5 points from those games.

What to do (2)
  • Only start a rated game when you are sure you have time to finish it; play unrated or daily games when you might be interrupted.
  • Check your connection and battery before a rated session, and play on even in bad positions: opponents at club level often let you back in.

i

Observation · Playing habits

You play worse right after a loss

Seen in your rapid games only, and not strong enough across all your games to call it a finding: it may be chance. In 38 games started within 15 minutes of a loss you scored 30% where your rating predicts 50%: 19 points per 100 games below your rating. Your other games: +4 per 100 games vs your rating.

What to do (3)
  • Stop rule: after any loss, wait at least 15 minutes before starting another game.
  • Use the break to find the move where the lost game turned; start the next game only once you know what went wrong.
  • If you catch yourself pressing 'New game' seconds after a loss, switch to puzzles instead.

Repeated mistake

5...e5 better 5...Nf6

9.0% winning chances lost · you played it in 6 games

After 5...e5, Stockfish's answer is 6.Nf3 h6 7.Qd5 Qf6. Stockfish rates the line −1.08 for you, against +0.08 after 5...Nf6: White's queen gets to d5 (7.Qd5), a square no pawn of yours can cover, and a few moves later you stand 0.38 pawns worse on king safety. Next time, ask which squares in your camp no pawn of yours can cover any more, and which enemy piece can reach them.

What 5...e5 allows
5...e5 6.Nf3 h6 7.Qd5 Qf6 8.a3 d6 9.Nc3 Be6 10.Qd3 Bxc4 11.Qxc4 Qe6 12.Nd5 Rc8 13.Be3 … (−1.08 for you)
Better: 5...Nf6
5...Nf6 6.Nc3 Qc7 7.Be2 Bc5 8.Nb3 Bb4 9.Qd3 O-O 10.Bg5 Qe5 11.Bd2 d5 (+0.08 for you)
  • d5 becomes a hole in your camp (no pawn of yours can cover it)

About king safety: Your king is safest behind pawns that haven't moved: each pawn you push in front of it stops guarding squares the enemy pieces can then use for a direct attack, and the pushed pawn itself becomes a target. Castle early, and move those pawns only for a concrete reason, not to stop a pin that isn't there yet. Lasker, Chess Strategy (Project Gutenberg #5614), Chapter VI, The Middle Game: Breaking up the King's Side ↗

How this report works

  • Every score is compared with what your rating predicts for each game (the Elo expected score for the rating gap), not with 50%. Beating lower-rated players is expected, so it is not counted as a strength. “+9 per 100 games vs your rating” means 9 game points more than your rating predicts in 100 games.
  • A strength or weakness needs enough games (about 8 for an opening with one colour, 25 for splits such as games after a loss) and a significance test that allows for how many things were tested. On players without any real strengths or weaknesses, a report lists about 0.2 false claims on average.
  • Observations (marked i) are patterns that did not pass that test, or plain facts: read them as context.
  • Findings are associations, not proof of a cause: “you score less late at night” does not say why.
  • The lists at the top show every strength and weakness, most important first (importance = how big the effect is × how sure we are); each finding is explained in its section.
  • chess.com Game Review accuracy and this report's engine accuracy use different formulas. Compare each only with itself.
